feedback: Written before this candidate has raced, so no result is stated for it. What I had to do in the controller: nothing beyond keeping the iteration 3 gains (kp 0.8, kd 0.15, ki 0, base_speed 1.5). The controller must stay fixed so that the mass change is the only variable. Evidence: iteration 6 (0.6 kg, same geometry otherwise) scored 55.45 against 69.18 at 0.8 kg. Its oval progress fell from 0.229 to 0.148 and oval steering oscillation fell from 0.120 to 0.101, so lighter mass made the robot steadier but slower to get through bends. Max error stayed at 0.060 to 0.067 m on every track in every run, so mass has not yet fixed the peak. Decision rules for the next race: if 1.0 kg scores above 69.18 with max_error falling, the heavier robot helps, so test mass 1.2 kg next, with everything else unchanged. If 1.0 kg scores below 69.18 while progress is unchanged, 0.8 kg is the local mass optimum, so move to wheel_radius. If steering_oscillation rises above about 0.17 on the s-bend or slalom, the heavier robot is under-damped, so change kd in the controller (for example 0.18), not the geometry.
requested_changes: If 1.0 kg scores above 69.18 with max_error falling, try mass 1.2 kg with everything else unchanged. Iteration 6 showed lower mass lowers the score (0.6 kg gave 55.45 against 69.18), so the trend is toward more mass, and the heavier end of the range is still untested.

If 1.0 kg scores below 69.18, keep mass 0.8 kg and try wheel_radius 0.035 m. Iterations 3 to 6 reached only 0.12 to 0.23 of the course, and a larger wheel should give more ground speed at the same PWM (a hypothesis from the progress shortfall, not yet measured).

If line_loss_events on the slalom stay at 2.0 (iterations 0, 3, 4, 5 and 6), try sensor_size 0.016 m on the 80 mm row as a single test. A larger footprint keeps readings above the 0.05 line-loss threshold for longer. Iteration 1 changed sensor size together with other variables, so this effect is not yet proven.
